props.title: My Little Chickadee

sections.content: My Little Chickadee (1940) marks a legendary pairing of two of Hollywood's most notorious personalities - Mae West and W.C. Fields. Their only collaboration showcases both stars' signature styles: West's sultry double entendres and Fields' misanthropic wit. The film cleverly plays with Western tropes while letting both performers deliver their iconic personas - West as the scandalous Flower Belle Lee and Fields as the fraudulent Cuthbert J. Twillie. Like Destry Rides Again (1939), it demonstrates how comedy could refresh tired Western formulas, though here through a more subversive, innuendo-laden approach.

sections.content: The film's importance extends beyond its star pairing - it represents a fascinating moment when the Production Code was being tested through clever wordplay and suggestion. West and Fields co-wrote the screenplay, loading it with double meanings that somehow slipped past censors. This approach influenced later comedians like Bob Hope and would resurface in films like Some Like It Hot (1959), which similarly used innuendo to push boundaries while maintaining plausible deniability.

Director Edward F. Cline, who directed many of Fields' best films including The Bank Dick (1940), manages the tricky balance of letting both stars shine without either overwhelming the other. The Western setting provides plenty of opportunities for both West's seductive swagger and Fields' pratfalls. While not as polished as later Western comedies like Cat Ballou (1965), it established a template for mixing comedy with Western elements that would influence films for decades. sections.content: My Little Chickadee helped establish the comedy Western as a viable genre, paving the way for films like Blazing Saddles (1974) and Support Your Local Sheriff (1969). Its willingness to lampoon Western conventions while still delivering genuine Western elements created a blueprint for genre parody that maintains affection for its source material. The film's influence can be seen in everything from The Paleface (1948) with Bob Hope to modern examples like Shanghai Noon (2000).
